title: Initial Management in Surgical Patients
subject: Surgery
summary: A step‑by‑step approach to stabilising a surgical patient in low‑resource settings, focusing on ABCs, fluid resuscitation, analgesia, and early decision‑making when investigations are limited.

sections.p: Initial management refers to the first hour of care after a surgical patient presents, aimed at preserving life, preventing deterioration and preparing for definitive treatment.
b: Identify life‑threatening problems before the exact diagnosis.
Use bedside assessment when imaging or labs are unavailable.

sections.p: Severity is judged by physiological derangement rather than anatomical extent. Common bedside scores: Shock Index (>0.9), qSOFA (≥2), and the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist for urgency.
b: Mild: stable vitals, no organ dysfunction.
Moderate: tachycardia, borderline BP, mild lactate rise.
Severe: hypotension, altered mental status, lactate >2 mmol/L.

sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals, the most frequent surgical emergencies are:
b: Perforated peptic ulcer (often H. pylori‑related).
Obstructed hernia (incarcerated inguinal/femoral).
Acute appendicitis with perforation.
Traumatic intra‑abdominal bleed.
Obstetric emergencies (ruptured ectopic, uterine rupture).
Infection‑related emergencies (TB abdomen, schistosomal colitis).

sections.p: Typical features include sudden severe pain, abdominal distension, vomiting, fever, and signs of systemic compromise.
b: Pain out of proportion to exam suggests ischemia.
Absent bowel sounds may indicate paralytic ileus.
Guarding or rigidity points to peritonitis.

t.b: Is the patient oxygenating? < 94 % triggers supplemental O₂.
Detect hypoglycaemia, especially in children or malnourished adults.
Screen for tissue hypoperfusion; >2 mmol/L suggests shock.
Detect free intra‑abdominal fluid when CT is not accessible.
Leukocytosis supports infection; anaemia may indicate bleed.
Guide fluid choice; correct severe derangements before surgery.

sections.p: Recognise early signs that demand urgent escalation.
b: Persistent hypotension despite 30 mL/kg fluids.
Altered mental status or GCS < 13.
Uncontrolled massive haemorrhage.
Severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.2).
Signs of compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, tense abdomen).

sections.p: A systematic ABC‑focused protocol works even when diagnostics are scarce.
b: Airway: clear obstruction, place a simple oral airway, consider nasopharyngeal airway if unconscious.
Breathing: give supplemental O₂ via nasal cannula or face mask to keep SpO₂ ≥ 94 %.
Circulation: obtain large‑bore IV (14‑16 G); give isotonic crystalloid 30 mL/kg rapidly, reassess BP and urine output.
If hypotension persists, repeat 15 mL/kg bolus; start norepinephrine infusion if available, otherwise dopamine.
Control pain with IV paracetamol or low‑dose morphine; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment suspected.
Give broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) after cultures only if it will not delay resuscitation.
Withhold oral intake until obstruction is ruled out; insert nasogastric tube for decompression if vomiting or distension.
Arrange urgent surgical review; if transfer is needed, stabilise and document vitals, fluids given, and labs performed.

sections.p: After stabilisation, monitor trends and plan definitive care.
b: Re‑measure vitals every 15 min until stable, then hourly.
Track urine output; aim for > 0.5 mL/kg/h.
Repeat lactate after 2 h; falling trend indicates adequate perfusion.
Educate on early presentation for abdominal pain, especially in high‑risk groups (e.g., chronic NSAID users, HIV‑positive patients).
Acute pancreatitis – pain radiates to back, serum amylase/lipase rise.
Severe malaria with abdominal pain – consider travel history, malaria smear.
Gynecologic torsion – pelvic pain, adnexal mass on bedside ultrasound.
Normal haemoglobin may mask acute bleed if chronic anaemia exists.
Lactate can be falsely low in patients on beta‑blockers.
FAST may miss retro‑peritoneal bleed; keep clinical suspicion high.

whenToSeekHelp: Systolic BP < 90 mmHg after two fluid boluses.
Rapidly rising abdominal girth with tense abdomen.

faq.a: They reduce bacterial load, lower risk of postoperative infection, and are lifesaving in septic patients.

faq.q: Can I give fluids to a patient with suspected bowel perforation?
faq.a: Yes, but limit to 30 mL/kg initially; excess fluids worsen oedema and may precipitate abdominal compartment syndrome.

faq.q: What if I have no vasopressor available?
faq.a: Give a second fluid bolus, consider low‑dose dopamine if cardiac output is low, and expedite transfer to a higher‑level centre.

exam: What are the first three actions you take for a patient with a suspected perforated ulcer presenting in shock? — ABCs, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, nasogastric decompression, early broad‑spectrum antibiotics.
How does the Shock Index help you decide on fluid resuscitation? — SI = HR/BP; >0.9 signals inadequate perfusion and need for aggressive fluids/vasopressors.
A patient with an incarcerated inguinal hernia is tachycardic but normotensive; what is your next step? — Give a fluid bolus, assess for evolving shock, and arrange urgent surgical review.
Why is it important to withhold oral intake before confirming obstruction? — Prevents vomiting, aspiration, and worsens distension; allows safe NG tube placement.
When is norepinephrine preferred over dopamine in septic shock? — In adults with persistent hypotension after fluids, norepinephrine achieves target MAP with fewer arrhythmias.
What bedside sign distinguishes peritonitis from simple ileus? — Guarding or rebound tenderness on palpation indicates peritoneal irritation.
How would you modify management if point‑of‑care lactate is unavailable? — Rely on clinical signs (cold extremities, delayed capillary refill) and urine output to gauge perfusion.
Explain why NSAIDs are avoided in a patient with suspected intra‑abdominal bleed. — They impair platelet function and can worsen bleeding.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic abdominal exam allow rapid identification of life‑threatening pathology when imaging is delayed or unavailable.
b: Onset: sudden vs gradual; exact time of pain start.
Pain character: colicky, constant, tearing, or out of proportion to exam.
Location and radiation: epigastric, periumbilical, RLQ, flank.
Associated symptoms: vomiting (bilious vs non‑bilious), obstipation, haematemesis, melena, fever, chills.
Past surgical or obstetric history: previous laparotomy, hernia repair, obstetric complications.
Risk factors: HIV, TB, schistosomiasis, alcohol, NSAID use, pregnancy, trauma.
Medication and substance use: anticoagulants, antiplatelets, herbal remedies.

t.b: Looks for distension, surgical scars, visible peristalsis, bruising; a tense, distended abdomen suggests obstruction or intra‑abdominal bleed.
Bowel sounds: hyperactive early obstruction, absent in ileus or peritonitis; high‑pitched squeaks may indicate early obstruction.
Tympany over gas‑filled loops; dullness suggests fluid, mass, or organomegaly; shifting dullness helps detect ascites but cannot quantify volume.
Voluntary guarding is protective; involuntary rigidity indicates peritonitis and warrants urgent escalation.
Pain on release of pressure suggests peritoneal irritation; a positive sign does not differentiate source.
Pain on deep inspiration with RUQ palpation indicates gallbladder inflammation; a negative test does not exclude other causes of RUQ pain.
Increased pain when tensing abdominal wall points to abdominal wall pathology; a negative sign suggests intra‑abdominal source.
Pain on passive extension of the hip suggests retroperitoneal irritation (e.g., appendicitis); a negative test does not rule it out.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select investigations that answer the key clinical questions; interpret results with locally relevant thresholds and have alternatives when resources are limited.
b: What is the haemodynamic status? – bedside vitals, capillary refill, lactate if POCT available.
Is there intra‑abdominal infection? – white cell count, CRP, bedside ultrasound for free fluid.
Is there obstruction or perforation? – plain abdominal X‑ray, focused ultrasound, if CT unavailable.
Is there organ dysfunction? – creatinine, bilirubin, urine output, mental status.

t.b: Answers whether tissue hypoperfusion persists after 30 mL/kg fluids; >2 mmol/L after adequate fluids signals ongoing shock and prompts vasopressor consideration.
Detects leukocytosis (>12 ×10⁹/L) suggesting infection; neutrophil left shift supports bacterial cause; anaemia may indicate chronic bleed.
Rises from baseline indicate acute kidney injury; interpret relative to pre‑illness value, not a fixed cut‑off.
Shows air‑fluid levels, dilated loops (>3 cm), free air under diaphragm; absence of air does not exclude perforation.
Detects free intraperitoneal fluid, gallbladder wall thickening, hydronephrosis; a negative FAST cannot rule out retroperitoneal bleed.
Acidosis (pH <7.2, base excess ≤‑6 mmol/L) indicates severe metabolic derangement; hyperkalaemia may signal renal failure.
Essential in women of reproductive age; positive test changes imaging choice and medication safety.
Identifies immunosuppression that may alter infection presentation and antibiotic choice.
Rely on clinical scoring (e.g., Shock Index >0.9) and bedside ultrasound; repeat clinical assessment frequently.

sections.p: Combine bedside findings with investigations to assign a working diagnosis and grade physiological derangement, which drives immediate management.
b: Diagnosis is based on the dominant clinical syndrome: perforated viscus, obstructed hernia, intra‑abdominal bleed, or obstetric catastrophe.

Severity grading uses physiological parameters: mild (stable vitals, lactate ≤2 mmol/L), moderate (tachycardia >100 bpm, SBP 90‑100 mmHg, lactate 2‑4 mmol/L), severe (SBP <90 mmHg, lactate >2 mmol/L after fluids, altered mental status).
Shock Index >0.9 supports significant shock but does not replace blood pressure assessment.
Organ dysfunction criteria: creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL from baseline, urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h, GCS <13, or need for vasopressors.
For intra‑abdominal infection, the Sepsis‑3 definition applies: suspected infection plus SOFA increase ≥2.

sections.p: Several non‑surgical or alternative surgical pathologies mimic the common emergencies; systematic comparison prevents mis‑triage.
b: Acute pancreatitis vs perforated ulcer – serum amylase/lipase high in pancreatitis; free air on X‑ray favors perforation.
Mesenteric ischemia vs simple obstruction – pain out of proportion, lactate >2 mmol/L, normal bowel sounds early; CT angiography confirms if available.
Ectopic pregnancy vs ruptured ovarian cyst – positive hCG, adnexal mass, free fluid on ultrasound; cyst rupture lacks intra‑uterine gestational sac.
Tuberculous peritonitis vs bacterial peritonitis – chronic low‑grade fever, ascitic fluid high protein, lymphocyte predominance; response to anti‑TB therapy differs.

t.b: Pain radiates to back, serum amylase/lipase >3× ULN; absence of free air on imaging helps separate from perforation.
Severe pain with minimal exam findings, lactate >2 mmol/L, risk factors (AF, atherosclerosis); CTA is definitive when available.
Positive urine hCG, adnexal mass on ultrasound, free pelvic fluid; absence of intra‑uterine sac distinguishes from miscarriage.
Chronic abdominal distension, ascitic fluid SAAG low, lymphocyte‑rich; PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis confirms.

sections.p: Initial management of any acute surgical emergency follows a rapid, reproducible ladder that secures the airway, circulatory stability, and pain control before definitive operative or non‑operative therapy.
b: 1. Assess airway, breathing, circulation; give high‑flow oxygen and protect airway if GCS < 13 or vomiting risk.
2. Obtain two large‑bore IV lines; give 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus while monitoring pulse, BP, mental status.
3. Re‑measure vitals after fluid; if MAP < 65 mmHg or persistent tachycardia despite fluids, start norepinephrine (or phenylephrine if tachyarrhythmia) and consider early vasopressor infusion.
4. Give broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics covering gram‑negative, gram‑positive and anaerobes (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole or piperacillin‑tazobactam) unless contraindicated.
5. Provide analgesia with opioid titration; avoid NSAIDs if bleeding risk or renal impairment.
6. Insert nasogastric tube for decompression if obstruction or perforation suspected; keep patient nil per os.
7. Arrange definitive treatment: emergency laparotomy, percutaneous drainage, or obstetric delivery as indicated.
8. Continuous monitoring: vitals q5 min, urine output, lactate, mental status; escalate to ICU or surgical referral if worsening.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Understanding the common adverse effects of the drugs used in the first hour prevents iatrogenic harm and guides rapid corrective actions.
b: Beta‑lactam antibiotics may cause allergic rash or anaphylaxis – stop drug, give antihistamine and epinephrine if needed.
Metronidazole can precipitate a disulfiram‑like reaction with alcohol – advise strict abstinence from alcohol during therapy.
Norepinephrine raises systemic vascular resistance; watch for peripheral ischemia – reduce dose or switch to vasopressin if signs appear.
Opioids depress respiration and may worsen CO₂ retention in COPD – monitor SpO₂, provide naloxone if severe depression occurs.
Crystalloid overload can cause pulmonary edema in patients with cardiac failure – limit to 20 mL/kg if signs of fluid overload appear.

sections.p: Early recognition of physiological deterioration triggers escalation to higher‑level care or operative intervention.
b: Persistent hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg) after 30 mL/kg fluids and norepinephrine → transfer to ICU or operating theatre.
Lactate > 2 mmol/L after initial resuscitation and rising trend → consider source control failure, add vasopressors, repeat imaging.
New onset oliguria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h) or rising creatinine from baseline → start renal protective measures, consider nephrology input.
GCS falling below 13 or new confusion → secure airway, consider intracranial cause, notify senior.
Severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.2, base excess ≤ ‑6 mmol/L) → increase perfusion, consider bicarbonate only if refractory.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities common in East African settings modify presentation, laboratory interpretation and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV infection may blunt fever and leukocytosis; CD4 count guides prophylactic antibiotics and opportunistic infection risk.
Active TB peritonitis presents with chronic ascites; GeneXpert on fluid if available, otherwise treat empirically for TB.
Severe malnutrition reduces albumin, exaggerating third‑space loss; give cautious fluid bolus and consider early albumin if available.
Pregnancy masks peritoneal signs and limits radiography; use bedside ultrasound, avoid teratogenic drugs, choose cefazolin + metronidazole for intra‑abdominal infection.
Diabetes predisposes to fungal infection and delayed wound healing; monitor glucose, avoid high‑dose steroids unless essential.
Chronic alcohol use raises risk of pancreatitis and coagulopathy; correct coagulopathy with fresh frozen plasma before surgery.
Renal failure limits use of nephrotoxic antibiotics (e.g., aminoglycosides) and requires dose adjustment of all renally cleared drugs.
Advanced age reduces physiological reserve; lower fluid thresholds, monitor for delirium, and avoid anticholinergic meds.

sections.p: Tailoring the first‑hour protocol to vulnerable populations ensures safety while preserving the core resuscitation principles.
b: Children: use weight‑based fluid bolus (20 mL/kg isotonic saline), avoid adult vasopressor doses, consider intra‑osseous access if IV fails.

Pregnant women: left lateral tilt, give crystalloid bolus, use cefazolin + metronidazole for intra‑abdominal infection, avoid teratogenic drugs, plan for possible emergency cesarean if obstetric cause.
Elderly: start with 15 mL/kg fluid, monitor for fluid overload, use norepinephrine as first vasopressor, assess for delirium, adjust antibiotics for renal function.
People with HIV: screen for opportunistic intra‑abdominal infections, use broader antimicrobial coverage, avoid high‑dose steroids, consider drug‑drug interactions with antiretrovirals.

Low‑resource settings: if lactate meter unavailable, use capillary refill, mental status and urine output as surrogates; use oral antibiotics when IV unavailable after initial bolus; rely on bedside ultrasound for free fluid.

t.a: What bedside history questions identify a perforated viscus?
t.b: Onset, character, radiation of pain; vomiting (bilious); last bowel movement; fever; risk factors (NSAID use, H. pylori).

t.a: How do you elicit guarding and what does a positive sign indicate?
t.b: Palpate abdomen gently then deeper; involuntary muscle spasm = peritoneal irritation, suggests perforation or severe inflammation.

t.a: If point‑of‑care lactate is unavailable, what surrogate guides resuscitation?
t.b: Use capillary refill > 3 seconds, altered mental status, urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h, and persistent tachycardia.

t.a: When is norepinephrine preferred over dopamine in septic shock?
t.b: When tachyarrhythmia is present or MAP cannot be achieved with fluids; norepinephrine has lower arrhythmogenic risk.

t.a: What is the first step for an incarcerated inguinal hernia with tachycardia but normal BP?
t.b: Give 30 mL/kg crystalloid, monitor vitals, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, arrange urgent surgical reduction.

t.a: How does pregnancy alter interpretation of serum creatinine?
t.b: Physiological GFR rise lowers baseline; a creatinine > 1.1 mg/dL may already indicate renal hypoperfusion.

t.a: What antibiotic regimen covers gram‑positive, gram‑negative and anaerobes for a perforated ulcer in pregnancy?
t.b: Cefazolin plus metronidazole; cefazolin covers gram‑positive, metronidazole covers anaerobes, and both are safe in pregnancy.

t.a: When should a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in COPD be intervened upon?
t.b: If rim > 2 cm or patient symptomatic; perform needle aspiration or small‑bore chest drain promptly.

t.a: What monitoring parameter signals need for vasopressor escalation despite fluids?
t.b: Persistent MAP < 65 mmHg after 30 mL/kg crystalloid with rising lactate > 2 mmol/L.

t.a: How does severe malnutrition affect fluid resuscitation?
t.b: Low oncotic pressure predisposes to pulmonary edema; give smaller fluid aliquots and reassess frequently.

facts: Shock Index (HR/SBP) >0.9 suggests significant circulatory compromise.
Lactate >2 mmol/L after 30 mL/kg fluid challenge signals ongoing tissue hypoperfusion.
Persistent SBP <90 mmHg despite fluids mandates vasopressor initiation.
GCS <13 is a red‑flag for altered mental status in acute surgical shock.
Base excess ≤‑6 mmol/L with pH <7.2 indicates severe metabolic acidosis.
Point‑of‑care ultrasound (FAST) can detect free intra‑abdominal fluid in trauma.
Broad‑spectrum intra‑abdominal sepsis coverage: ceftriaxone + metronidazole (adds gram‑positive coverage with ampicillin if needed).
Tranexamic acid is indicated only for major trauma bleeding within 3 h of injury.
In pregnant patients with suspected perforated ulcer, give cefazolin + metronidazole (covers gram‑positive, gram‑negative, anaerobes).
Needle aspiration or small‑bore chest drain is first‑line for a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax ≥2 cm in COPD.

mnemonics.t: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma – screens for free fluid in perihepatic, perisplenic, pelvic, and pericardial spaces.
Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure – systematic initial assessment in any surgical emergency.

vivas.q: What are the first three actions for a patient with a suspected perforated peptic ulcer?
vivas.a: 1) Secure airway and give high‑flow oxygen. 2) Insert large‑bore IV and give 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus. 3) Obtain bedside upright chest/abdominal X‑ray or FAST to look for free air or fluid.

vivas.q: How does the Shock Index guide fluid resuscitation?
vivas.a: A SI >0.9 indicates inadequate stroke volume; after an initial 30 mL/kg bolus, if SI remains >0.9, consider early vasopressor rather than repeated fluids.

vivas.q: A patient with an incarcerated inguinal hernia is tachycardic but normotensive. What is your next step?
vivas.a: Give 30 mL/kg crystalloid, reassess vitals and SI; if SI >0.9 or lactate >2 mmol/L, prepare for urgent surgical reduction and consider vasopressor support.

vivas.q: Why must oral intake be withheld in a suspected bowel obstruction?
vivas.a: Oral intake can increase intraluminal pressure, risk of perforation, and vomiting; NPO status reduces aspiration risk and allows accurate assessment of nasogastric output.

vivas.q: When is norepinephrine preferred over dopamine in septic shock?
vivas.a: Norepinephrine is first‑line for septic shock because it raises MAP with less tachyarrhythmia; dopamine is reserved for bradycardic patients or when renal perfusion is a priority.

vivas.q: What bedside sign distinguishes peritonitis from simple ileus?
vivas.a: Rebound tenderness (Blumberg sign) with guarding indicates peritonitis; ileus shows absent or hypoactive bowel sounds without localized tenderness.

vivas.q: How would you modify management if point‑of‑care lactate is unavailable?
vivas.a: Rely on clinical markers: persistent hypotension, altered mental status, capillary refill >2 s, and urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h to decide on vasopressor initiation.

vivas.q: Explain why NSAIDs are avoided in a patient with suspected intra‑abdominal bleed.
vivas.a: NSAIDs inhibit platelet aggregation and can worsen bleeding; they also impair renal perfusion in hypovolaemic states.

vivas.q: A 30‑year‑old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding, Hb 9 g/dL, iron deficiency – which medical therapy is most appropriate initially?
vivas.a: Tranexamic acid during menses reduces blood loss and is first‑line for acute heavy menstrual bleeding when anemia is present.

vivas.q: Newborn with right‑sided full‑thickness abdominal wall defect, exposed bowel, no membrane – what is the most appropriate immediate management?
vivas.a: Cover the exposed bowel with sterile, moist, non‑adhesive dressing, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and arrange urgent surgical repair (omphalocele vs gastroschisis distinction).

vivas.q: 31‑year‑old primigravida at 34 weeks reports fetal movements reduced from 10 to 2 per hour – next step?
vivas.a: Perform immediate bedside cardiotocography; if non‑reassuring, arrange urgent obstetric review and possible emergency delivery.

vivas.q: 62‑year‑old post‑distal pancreatectomy day 3 with mild nausea, early satiety, soft abdomen, active sounds – initial management strategy?
vivas.a: Advance diet slowly (clear fluids to soft diet), ensure adequate analgesia, monitor for delayed gastric emptying, and check electrolytes; no imaging needed unless symptoms worsen.

vivas.q: 58‑year‑old man with prior appendectomy presents with colicky pain, vomiting, obstipation, X‑ray shows dilated small bowel loops – next step?
vivas.a: Insert nasogastric tube, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid, obtain electrolytes, and arrange urgent surgical review for possible adhesive small‑bowel obstruction.

vivas.q: 40‑year‑old woman with 5 cm pericolic abscess, no free air – what is the most appropriate initial management?
vivas.a: Start broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics covering gram‑negative, gram‑positive and anaerobes; arrange percutaneous drainage if feasible; defer surgery unless clinical deterioration.

vivas.q: 75‑year‑old man with decompensated heart failure and small pleural effusion – most appropriate initial management?
vivas.a: Optimize heart failure with diuretics and oxygen; perform bedside ultrasound to confirm effusion size; if symptomatic, consider thoracentesis, but treat HF first.

vivas.q: Outline comprehensive initial management of sepsis (Hour‑1 bundle).
vivas.a: 1) Measure lactate; 2) Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics; 3) Give broad‑spectrum antibiotics within 1 h; 4) Begin 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus; 5) Apply vasopressors if MAP <65 mmHg after fluids.

vivas.q: Outline initial management principles for a patient presenting with jaundice.
vivas.a: Assess for haemolysis, obstruction, hepatitis; obtain LFTs, bilirubin fractions, ultrasound; start vitamin K if coagulopathy; treat underlying cause; avoid hepatotoxic drugs.

vivas.q: First 5‑15 minutes for a child in shock according to goal‑directed algorithm?
vivas.a: 1) Airway with chin‑lift, suction; 2) Give 20 mL/kg isotonic fluid bolus; 3) Re‑assess perfusion (cap refill, pulses, mental status); 4) If still shocked, repeat bolus once; 5) Start inotrope if MAP remains low.

vivas.q: Clinical signs and initial management of neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS).
vivas.a: Signs: tachypnoea, nasal flaring, grunting, ground‑glass X‑ray. Management: CPAP or nasal ventilation, early surfactant via endotracheal tube, maintain temperature, monitor blood gases.

mcqs.q: Which bedside test is most reliable for detecting free intra‑abdominal fluid in a trauma patient when CT is unavailable?
o: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST)
mcqs.e: FAST is rapid, non‑invasive, and detects fluid in peritoneal spaces.

mcqs.q: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks presents with a perforated ulcer. Which antibiotic regimen is appropriate?
mcqs.e: Cefazolin covers gram‑positive organisms; metronidazole adds anaerobic coverage needed for intra‑abdominal infection.

mcqs.q: In a patient with suspected small‑bowel obstruction, which finding most strongly suggests strangulation?
o: Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to exam
mcqs.e: Pain out of proportion indicates ischemia/strangulation, a surgical emergency.

cases.v: A 28‑year‑old male presents with sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, rigid abdomen, and hypotension (BP 80/55). No imaging available.

qs.a: Airway with high‑flow O₂, large‑bore IV, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, bedside FAST or upright chest X‑ray to look for free air, and early broad‑spectrum antibiotics.

qs.q: Which bedside sign helps differentiate perforated ulcer from pancreatitis?
qs.a: Rigidity with rebound tenderness suggests peritonitis from perforation; pancreatitis often has diffuse tenderness without guarding.

qs.q: If lactate is 3 mmol/L after fluids, what is the next step?
qs.a: Start norepinephrine infusion to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg while arranging definitive surgical repair.

cases.v: A 62‑year‑old woman, 3 days post‑distal pancreatectomy, reports nausea, early satiety, and reduced oral intake. Abdomen is soft, bowel sounds present.

qs.q: What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
qs.a: Delayed gastric emptying (post‑operative gastroparesis) is common after pancreatic surgery.
Advance diet gradually, provide anti‑emetics, ensure adequate analgesia, monitor electrolytes and fluid balance, and reassess for obstruction if symptoms persist.
If nausea worsens, abdominal distension develops, or vitals become unstable, obtain an abdominal X‑ray or ultrasound to rule out anastomotic leak or obstruction.

mistakes: Repeating fluid boluses despite a Shock Index >0.9 instead of starting vasopressors.
Using lactate >2 mmol/L alone as a trigger for vasopressors without confirming hypotension.
Prescribing tranexamic acid for any bleeding; it is limited to major trauma or obstetric hemorrhage.
Choosing cefazolin alone for intra‑abdominal infection in pregnancy, missing anaerobic coverage.
Assuming a small secondary pneumothorax in COPD can be observed; guidelines require aspiration or drainage.
Interpreting a base excess >‑6 mmol/L as severe acidosis; the correct threshold is ≤‑6 mmol/L.
Relying on a single bedside sign to rule out peritonitis; combine guarding, rebound, and systemic signs.
Neglecting to cover gram‑positive organisms when using ceftriaxone + metronidazole for intra‑abdominal sepsis.
